issues.legal_issue: A bill passed by a legislative assembly that was later dissolved did not lapse when a successor assembly reconsidered and passed it before presidential assent.
material_facts: The bill had been passed by an earlier legislative assembly, which was then dissolved.
A successor legislative assembly reconsidered and passed the bill, after which the President assented to it.
issues.conclusion: The bill did not lapse and validly became law upon presidential assent.
issues.legal_principle: The Court followed Purushothaman Nambudiri v. State of Kerala, holding that the bill's passage by the earlier assembly did not prevent the successor assembly from reconsidering and passing it under Article 201 before presidential assent.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_enactment and earlier_assembly_dissolved and successor_assembly_reconsidered_and_passed_bill and presidential_assent_given

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_enactment: The proceeding challenges the validity of an enactment made through a legislative process.
predicates.earlier_assembly_dissolved: The assembly that first passed the bill was dissolved before the bill received presidential assent.
predicates.successor_assembly_reconsidered_and_pass: A successor assembly reconsidered and passed the bill before presidential assent.
predicates.presidential_assent_given: The President assented to the bill after the successor assembly passed it.
predicates.bill_validly_enacted: The bill became a valid law upon presidential assent.

issues.definition: When an enactment challenge concerns a bill passed by a dissolved assembly, the bill is validly enacted if a successor assembly reconsiders and passes it before presidential assent.

issues.legal_issue: A land-reform law providing for acquisition and redistribution of land was not colourable legislation merely because the compensation schemes involved deductions from purchase price or market value.
material_facts: The law provided for the State to acquire landowners' interests and excess land before potentially assigning land to tenants or eligible landless persons.
The law separately prescribed compensation for acquired interests and excess land, while the amounts payable by later assignees were determined under separate provisions.
Any surplus from purchase prices after compensation was to be placed in a rehabilitation fund for people affected by the law.
The law's rules also purported to make some persons who were not affected by the law eligible for assistance from the fund.
issues.conclusion: The law could not be struck down as colourable legislation beyond the State Legislature's competence on the ground that it indirectly took compensation money for State revenue; however, rules extending fund benefits to persons not affected by the law were ultra vires the provision establishing the fund.
issues.legal_principle: Under K. C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa, colourable legislation turns on legislative competence and whether a legislature has in substance done indirectly what it could not do directly, not on legislative motive. The Court held that the law's acquisition and redistribution scheme fell within the relevant legislative powers, and that compensation was what the law prescribed rather than an amount first due to landholders and then diverted. Article 31(2) precluded a challenge to the adequacy of compensation. The fund provision, section 80, authorized assistance to persons affected by the law, so rules extending assistance beyond that class exceeded the enabling provision.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a law that reforms land ownership.
predicates.law_acquires_and_redistributes_land: The law provides for State acquisition of land interests followed by possible assignment to tenants or other eligible recipients.
predicates.compensation_separately_defined_by_law: The law itself specifies the compensation payable for the acquired interests, separately from any price later paid by an assignee.
predicates.surplus_fund_reserved_for_affected_perso: Any surplus is directed to a fund whose permitted beneficiaries are persons affected by the law.
predicates.law_not_colourable_on_compensation_diver: The law is not colourable legislation merely because its compensation provisions produce a surplus or use deductions in calculating compensation.

issues.definition: A land-reform law is not colourable on a compensation-diversion theory where it acquires and redistributes land, separately defines compensation, and directs any surplus to a fund for affected persons.

issues.legal_issue: Rules establishing assistance from a rehabilitation fund could not extend eligibility to persons whom the enabling law limited the fund to helping.
material_facts: The law established a rehabilitation fund to help persons affected by the law who were eligible under rules.
Some rules extended grants or loans to persons who were not affected by the law.
issues.conclusion: The rules were ultra vires to the extent that they made persons not affected by the law eligible for grants or loans from the fund.
issues.legal_principle: Section 80 limited the fund's purpose to rendering assistance to persons affected by the law and eligible under the rules. Rules made under that section could not enlarge the statutory class of beneficiaries.

predicates.challenge_to_subordinate_rules: The proceeding challenges rules made under an enabling law.
predicates.enabling_law_limits_fund_beneficiaries_t: The enabling law restricts the fund's beneficiaries to persons affected by the law.
predicates.rules_include_unaffected_persons: The rules make persons unaffected by the law eligible for the fund's assistance.
predicates.rules_invalid_to_extent_they_include_una: The rules are beyond the enabling law to the extent that they include persons outside its permitted beneficiary class.

issues.definition: Rules governing a fund are invalid to the extent that they make unaffected persons eligible when the enabling law limits assistance to affected persons.

issues.legal_issue: Ryotwari holdings were not estates protected from constitutional challenge by the constitutional protection for laws concerning estates.
material_facts: The lands were held on ryotwari pattas in an area formerly within the Madras State.
On the relevant constitutional date, the Madras Estates Land Act defined estates but did not include ryotwari holdings.
The challenged law affected those ryotwari lands.
issues.conclusion: The ryotwari lands were not estates within Article 31A(2)(a), so the law was not protected from challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31 insofar as it applied to those lands.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A(2)(a) adopts the meaning of estate in the existing law relating to land tenures in the relevant area. The Court relied on the definition in the Madras Estates Land Act, which excluded ryotwari holdings, and referred to State of Bihar v. Rameshwar Pratap Narain Singh. Justices Ram Ram Narain Medhi v. State of Bombay and Atma Ram v. State of Punjab were also referred to in the separate opinion concerning the scope of the term.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a land-reform law.
predicates.land_held_on_ryotwari_tenure: The affected land is held under a ryotwari tenure.
predicates.existing_land_tenure_law_excludes_ryotwa: The existing land-tenure law applicable to the area defines estates without including ryotwari holdings.
predicates.estate_protection_unavailable_for_ryotwa: The affected ryotwari land does not receive constitutional protection available to laws concerning estates.

issues.definition: Ryotwari land is not protected as an estate where the existing land-tenure law applicable to it excludes ryotwari holdings from that category.

issues.legal_issue: Exempting certain plantation crops from land-acquisition and ceiling rules while excluding comparable plantation crops violated equal protection, and the discriminatory plantation provisions could not be severed from the law as applied to the affected ryotwari lands.
material_facts: The law exempted plantations of specified crops from provisions concerning acquisition of landowners' interests and land ceilings, while areca and pepper plantations received no equivalent exemption.

The evidence before the Court showed that areca and pepper plantations could involve substantial investment, delayed returns and plantation-scale cultivation, including large and organized operations.
The State gave no sufficient reason for treating those crops differently from the exempted plantation crops in light of the objects of the law.
The plantation exemptions affected the operation of the law's principal acquisition and ceiling schemes.
issues.conclusion: The plantation provisions violated Article 14; they could not be severed from the rest of the law, which was therefore invalid insofar as it applied to the relevant ryotwari lands.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14 and the classification principles summarized in Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar, a classification must rest on an intelligible differentia related to the law's object; the presumption of constitutionality cannot supply an undisclosed basis where none appears in the law or surrounding circumstances. The Court considered the land-reform objectives and the plantation-exemption criteria discussed in the Second and Third Five Year Plans. Because the legislature would not have intended the central acquisition and ceiling schemes to operate by breaking up the exempted plantations, the discriminatory provisions were not severable.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a land-reform law.
predicates.some_plantation_crops_exempted_but_compa: The law exempts some plantation crops from its acquisition or ceiling rules while leaving comparable plantation crops subject to them.
predicates.no_relevant_basis_for_crop_distinction: The record shows no intelligible distinction related to the law's purposes that justifies the different treatment.
predicates.plantation_exemptions_integral_to_law: The exemptions are integral to the operation of the law's principal acquisition and ceiling schemes and cannot be severed without defeating legislative intent.
predicates.law_invalid_as_applied_to_covered_ryotwa: The law is unconstitutional insofar as it applies to the affected ryotwari land.

issues.definition: A land-reform law is invalid as applied to affected ryotwari land where it gives integral exemptions to some plantation crops but not comparable crops without a relevant basis for the distinction.

issues.legal_issue: A land ceiling based on separate individual and artificially defined family standards violated equal protection when it caused similarly situated landholders to surrender unequal amounts of land without justification.
material_facts: The law set one ceiling for an adult unmarried person and a different ceiling for a family defined by reference to a husband, wife and unmarried minor children or such of them as existed.
That definition did not correspond to the family forms recognized under the personal laws relevant to the State.
The different standards could cause persons with equal landholdings, including an adult unmarried person and a minor orphan, to retain different amounts of land.
The State provided no justification for the resulting difference.
issues.conclusion: The ceiling provision violated Article 14, and because it formed the basis of the entire ceiling chapter, that chapter was invalid in its application to the affected ryotwari lands.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits classifications that produce unequal treatment without a rational basis connected to the law's purpose. The Court examined the actual consequences of the ceiling scheme rather than its facial application to each defined category, and held that the artificial family definition combined with separate standards produced unjustified discrimination.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_ceiling: The proceeding challenges a statutory land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.ceiling_uses_distinct_individual_and_fam: The scheme applies different land limits to individuals and families.
predicates.family_category_artificially_defined: The statutory family category does not correspond to the family forms relevant under applicable personal law.
predicates.equal_landholdings_produce_unequal_retai: The scheme causes persons with equal landholdings to retain different amounts of land, without a justification for the difference.
predicates.ceiling_scheme_unconstitutional: The land-ceiling scheme violates equal protection.

issues.definition: A ceiling scheme is unconstitutional where distinct individual and artificially defined family standards cause equally situated landholders to retain unequal land without justification.

issues.legal_issue: Progressively reducing compensation rates for larger property valuations, without a relevant basis connected to the law's purposes, discriminated between persons whose property was acquired.
material_facts: The law calculated compensation by applying progressively lower rates to higher slabs of purchase price or market value.
The reduction depended on the total valuation of the property, rather than a difference in the nature of the property being acquired.
The State relied on an analogy to progressive taxation, but the Court found no relevant basis for applying that principle to compensation for acquired property.
issues.conclusion: The majority held that the progressive compensation cuts violated Article 14 and, because compensation provisions were pervasive, the law was invalid insofar as it applied to the affected ryotwari lands. Justice Sarkar dissented on the validity of the progressive compensation rates.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 requires an intelligible differentia rationally related to the law's objects. The majority held that progressive taxation principles did not justify paying different compensation rates for property acquired by the State merely because one person's property had a higher valuation. It relied on the reasoning of the Special Bench in Kameshwar Singh v. State of Bihar, which rejected progressive compensation rates as discriminatory. Justice Sarkar's separate opinion considered ability to bear loss a relevant basis and would have upheld the rates.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compensation: The proceeding challenges a statutory compensation scheme for acquired property.
predicates.compensation_rate_decreases_as_property_: The scheme applies lower compensation rates to higher valuation slabs.
predicates.property_differs_only_in_extent_or_value: The acquired properties are of the same relevant kind and differ only in their size or valuation.
predicates.no_relevant_basis_for_different_rates: No intelligible basis connected to the law's purposes justifies the different compensation rates.
predicates.progressive_compensation_scheme_unconsti: The progressive compensation scheme violates equal protection.

issues.definition: A progressive compensation scheme is unconstitutional where the rate falls as valuation rises, the properties differ only in extent or value, and no relevant basis justifies the difference.
